title: Convexity and unconstrained optimization
rows: NLP session 1
2105623 Optimization of Chemical Processes
Geometry, derivatives, and numerical steps

title: Learning goals
rows: Classify convex sets and convex functions.
Compute gradient descent and Newton steps.
Check a numerical result using derivatives and geometry.

title: The three-hour session
rows: 60 min: convexity, examples, and short exercises
10 min break, then 75 min: unconstrained methods
35 min: Python lab, practice, and closing questions

title: The NLP problem
rows: Minimize a scalar function f(x) over its domain.
Unconstrained: no additional equality or inequality constraints.
Convexity describes geometry, independent of the variable count.

title: Convex sets
rows: Every segment between two feasible points stays in the set.
z = θx + (1−θ)y, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.
Half-spaces, balls, and their intersections are convex.

title: A nonconvex feasible set
rows: Annulus: 1 ≤ x₁² + x₂² ≤ 4.
The points (−1.5,0) and (1.5,0) are feasible.
Their midpoint (0,0) lies in the hole.

title: Set exercise
rows: C₁: x₁ ≥ 0, x₂ ≥ 0, x₁+x₂ ≤ 4.
C₂: x₁²+x₂² ≥ 1.
Which set is convex? Give a reason or counterexample.

title: Set exercise: solution
rows: C₁ is the intersection of three half-spaces.
For C₂, use p=(−1,0) and q=(1,0).
Both pass, but (p+q)/2=(0,0) violates x₁²+x₂² ≥ 1.

title: A convex function and its chord
rows: The graph lies below every chord joining two graph points.
The domain must also be convex.
Convexity compares function values along line segments.

title: The convexity inequality
rows: The left side evaluates f at an interpolated input.
The right side interpolates the two endpoint values.

title: Example: f(x)=x²
rows: Choose x=−1, y=3, and θ=1/2.
Midpoint value: f(1)=1.
Average endpoint value: [f(−1)+f(3)]/2=5. Thus 1 ≤ 5.

title: A counterexample for nonconvexity
rows: q(x)=(x²−1)² on the real line.
The midpoint inequality would require 1 ≤ 0, which is false.

title: Convex, strictly convex, and strongly convex
rows: Convex: the chord inequality may allow equality.
Strictly convex: strict inequality for distinct endpoints and 0<θ<1.
For C² f: strongly convex if H(x) ⪰ mI everywhere, for a fixed m>0.

title: The Hessian test
rows: Assume f is twice continuously differentiable on an open convex domain.
f is convex exactly when H(x) ⪰ 0 at every point in that domain.
Positive curvature at one point alone does not prove global convexity.

title: Reading a symmetric Hessian
rows: H ⪰ 0: dᵀHd ≥ 0 for every direction d.
Equivalently, every eigenvalue is nonnegative.
Mixed eigenvalue signs mean opposite curvature directions.

title: Example: a convex quadratic
rows: H is constant, with eigenvalues 2 and 8.
Both are positive, so f is strongly convex on R².

title: A global certificate from the gradient
rows: For differentiable convex f: f(y) ≥ f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y−x).
If ∇f(x*)=0, then f(y) ≥ f(x*) for every y in the domain.
Strict convexity gives at most one minimizer.

title: Why local minima are global in a convex problem
rows: Suppose a feasible y has f(y)<f(x*).
Points z=(1−t)x*+ty remain feasible and can lie arbitrarily close to x*.
Convexity gives f(z)<f(x*), contradicting local minimality.

title: Existence and uniqueness are separate
rows: Strict convexity means at most one minimizer, if one exists.
f(x)=exp(x) is strictly convex on R.
Its infimum is 0, but no finite x attains 0.

title: Convex optimization problems
rows: Minimize a convex objective over a convex feasible set.
Standard form: convex inequalities gᵢ(x)≤0 and affine equalities.
For maximization, a concave objective over a convex set is the matching case.

title: Classification exercise
rows: A: minimize x⁴ on R. B: minimize −x² on R.
C: minimize (x²−1)² on R.
Classify convexity, existence, and uniqueness of each minimizer.

title: Classification exercise: solution
rows: A: strictly convex, unique global minimum x=0, value 0.
B: concave and unbounded below. x=0 is a maximum.
C: nonconvex, two global minima x=−1 and x=1, value 0.

title: Derivatives and local change
rows: Gradient g=∇f collects first derivatives.
f(x+p) ≈ f(x)+gᵀp for small p.
The Hessian adds the quadratic term ½pᵀHp.

title: Stationary points and curvature
rows: At an interior local minimum of differentiable f, ∇f=0.
At a C² local minimum, H ⪰ 0 is necessary.
At a stationary point, H ≻ 0 is sufficient for a strict local minimum.

title: A stationary saddle point
rows: s(x,y)=x²−y², with ∇s(0,0)=0.
Along y=0: s=x²>0 for x≠0.
Along x=0: s=−y²<0 for y≠0.

title: A zero Hessian can be inconclusive
rows: At x=0, x⁴ and −x⁴ both have f′=0 and f″=0.
x⁴ has a strict minimum at 0.
−x⁴ has a strict maximum at 0. Higher-order behavior matters.

title: The shared quadratic example
rows: H=diag(2,8). Initial point x₀=(3,0)ᵀ.

title: The exact solution as a reference
rows: The unique solution is x*=(1,−2)ᵀ, with f(x*)=0.
Both squared terms are nonnegative, giving an independent certificate.

title: The negative gradient direction
rows: Choose p₀=−g₀=(−4,−16)ᵀ.
The direction is perpendicular to the local contour.

title: Why −g is a descent direction
rows: Directional derivative: gᵀp.
For p=−g≠0, gᵀp=−‖g‖²<0.
Here g₀ᵀp₀=−4²−16²=−272. Small positive steps reduce f.

title: The iterative update
rows: xₖ₊₁=xₖ+αₖpₖ, with αₖ>0.
The direction pₖ and the step size αₖ play different roles.
Today: fixed-step gradient descent and full Newton steps on selected examples.

title: The gradient descent path
rows: With α=0.1, the v error contracts faster than the u error.
The path approaches (1,−2), while the gradient approaches zero.
A decreasing objective alone does not identify the type of stationary point.

title: Step size changes the behavior
rows: For this quadratic, convergence from every start requires 0<α<0.25.
At α=0.25, the v error changes sign without shrinking.
At α=0.30, a nonzero v error grows in magnitude.

title: Derivation of the step-size interval
rows: Let eᵤ=u−1 and eᵥ=v+2.
eᵤ,new=(1−2α)eᵤ and eᵥ,new=(1−8α)eᵥ.
Both errors shrink when |1−2α|<1 and |1−8α|<1, giving 0<α<1/4.

title: Stopping and checking a result
rows: Use a gradient tolerance, an iteration limit, and finite-value checks.
Small steps can also reflect poor scaling or stagnation.
Report x, f(x), ‖∇f(x)‖, termination reason, and curvature.

title: Practice: a larger gradient step
rows: Use the same x₀=(3,0) and g₀=(4,16).
Take one step with α=0.2.
Calculate x₁ and f(x₁). Did either coordinate cross the minimizer?

title: Practice solution: α=0.2
rows: v crosses −2, but f falls from 20 to 7.2.

title: The Newton quadratic model
rows: m(p)=f(x)+gᵀp+½pᵀHp
Stationarity of m gives g+Hp=0.
Solve Hp=−g for p, then form xnew=x+p.

title: Newton direction at the initial point
rows: At x₀=(3,0), H=diag(2,8) and g₀=(4,16).
The two equations are 2pᵤ=−4 and 8pᵥ=−16.
Therefore p=(−2,−2). Solve the system instead of forming H⁻¹.

title: Newton update and verification
rows: This positive-definite quadratic reaches its exact minimizer in one full step.

title: When the one-step result applies
rows: For f(x)=½xᵀHx+cᵀx+r with constant H≻0:
Hp=−(Hx+c) implies x+p=−H⁻¹c=x*.
Nonquadratic functions have higher-order terms, so further iterations are usually needed.

title: Newton on a nonquadratic function
rows: r(x)=x⁴+x². At x₀=1: r′=6 and r″=14.
r(x₁)=1040/2401≈0.433153, down from 2. The minimum is still at 0.

title: Newton can move uphill in a nonconvex region
rows: q rises from 0.9216 to about 0.999339. Here gp>0.

title: A direction needs a descent check
rows: Before stepping, inspect gᵀp. A negative value indicates local descent.
If H≻0 and g≠0, Newton gives gᵀp=−gᵀH⁻¹g<0.
An indefinite Hessian may require a modified direction or a trust-region method.

title: Scaling and elongated contours
rows: Example: F=e₁²+100e₂² has Hessian eigenvalues 2 and 200.
The curvature ratio is 100. A single fixed step must respect the steep direction.
With z₁=e₁ and z₂=10e₂, F=z₁²+z₂².

title: Gradient descent and Newton
rows: Gradient descent uses first derivatives and a chosen step size.
Newton also uses curvature and solves a linear system.
Both require stopping checks. Nonconvex problems need additional interpretation.

title: Python lab: workflow
rows: 1. Define f, its gradient, and its Hessian.
2. Trace gradient descent and compare fixed step sizes.
3. Verify Newton, then classify nonconvex stationary points.

title: Lab 1: functions and derivative checks
rows: Use NumPy arrays in the fixed order [u,v].
At [3,0], expect f=20, gradient=[4,16], and Hessian=diag(2,8).
Compare analytic derivatives against central finite differences.

title: Lab 2: a gradient descent trace
rows: Start at [3,0], with α=0.1.
Expected first values: 20.0000, 3.2000, 1.6640.
Store each iterate and objective before checking convergence.

title: Lab 3: step-size experiments
rows: Keep x₀, tolerance, and iteration cap fixed across runs.
Report convergence, oscillation, or growth using the trace.

title: Lab 4: Newton and a reference solver
rows: Compute p=np.linalg.solve(H(x), −grad(x)).
One full quadratic step must give [1,−2], f=0.
Optional: compare with scipy.optimize.minimize using analytic derivatives.

title: Lab 5: nonconvex starting points
rows: For q(x)=(x²−1)², compare starts −1.5, −0.2, 0, 0.2, and 1.5.
Use gradient descent with α=0.05, then inspect q′ and q″.
The start x₀=0 can stop immediately at a local maximum.

title: Independent practice
rows: A. Minimize h=x²+2xy+3y²−4x−8y+7. Find H, eigenvalues, and x*.
B. Take one Newton step for r=x⁴+x² from x₀=2.
C. Explain why f′(0)=f″(0)=0 cannot identify a minimum.

title: Practice A: coupled quadratic solution
rows: H is shown at right; its eigenvalues are 4±2√2>0.
Stationarity gives x+y=2 and x+3y=4, hence (x*,y*)=(1,1).
h(1,1)=1. Positive-definite H certifies the unique global minimum.

title: Practice B and C: worked answers
rows: x₁=1.28, with r(x₁)=4.32275456, down from 20.
C. x⁴ and −x⁴ share zero first and second derivatives at 0, but have opposite extrema.

title: Closing questions
rows: 1. Does a positive Hessian at one point prove global convexity?
2. What happens at α=0.25 for the shared quadratic from [3,0]?
3. Why can Newton increase q at x=0.2?

title: Closing answers
rows: 1. No. The convexity Hessian test requires the whole open convex domain.
2. The v error alternates without shrinking, so the method does not reach x*.
3. q″(0.2)<0 gives an ascent Newton direction: gp>0.
